abstract: In the last fifteen years, manufacturing systems have undergone a profound transformation driven by Industry 4.0 technologies. The integration of smart resources and robots, sensors, and digital platforms offers companies the opportunity to make more informed assessments, adapt decisions in real-time, and ultimately achieve better performance. Yet, this integration has also introduced new challenges in the management and optimization of industrial processes, particularly in operation scheduling. The robotic resource studied in the paper is a complex welding cell comprising several collaborating components: three loading stations, a robotic arm responsible for picking up and transporting parts, two different welding machines, and a positioner designed to hold a part during processing. The main objective is to minimize both the makespan of all parts and their tardiness. To this end, this paper proposes a mathematical formulation for an optimization model as well as a scheduling agent based on a dynamic Graph Neural Network (GNN), trained with an adapted e-greedy deep Q-learning algorithm. In addition to the GNN-based policy, our agent utilizes a custom decision simulator to generate dates and movements, respecting all system constraints and logic. For large instances, our agent requires between 0.9 and 2.35 seconds to complete. Yet, the solving stage is a search process that includes a local improvement heuristic: the actual GNN-based agent only needs 0.07 to 0.14 seconds to construct a single solution. The memory usage is negligible, even during training. In contrast, the mathematical model, optimized via a constraint programming solver, used the maximum allowed computation time and memory (24 hours and 185 GB RAM) to find its best solution. For small instances where the mathematical model achieves optimal solutions, our agent reached a median deviation of 6.64%. For large-sized problems (for which the mathematical model only finds feasible solutions), the agent outperformed the mathematical model for 64% of the instances and achieved a median deviation of -2.82%.

LLM Agent-driven Automated DFA Assessment with Fine-tuning and AAS-based RAG
abstract: Design for Assembly (DFA) is a key methodology for controlling manufacturing costs. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate DFA evaluation, general-purpose models lack the required domain knowledge and reliable data access, making them prone to factual "hallucinations" and unsuitable for rigorous engineering assessments. To address these limitations, we introduce an automated DFA evaluation framework using an LLM Agent. Our "Controller-Agent-Tool" architecture coordinates a dual-core AI engine: (1) A domain-expert DFA-LLM, fine-tuned with a progressive strategy combining Domain-specific Continual Pre-training (D-CPT) with instructions from our new open-source DFA dataset. (2) An AAS-based hybrid retrieval system built on the Asset Administration Shell standard, which uses a dual-path approach—vector retrieval for semantic queries and a knowledge graph for exact parameter lookups—to handle heterogeneous industrial data. On DFA-Bench, the first public benchmark we developed, our expert model achieved 93\% accuracy. Our hybrid retrieval system reached a 91.4\% exact match rate on factual queries, substantially surpassing baseline models. This work contributes: (1) a systematic Agent solution for automated DFA, (2) the first public DFA benchmark, (3) an advanced retrieval strategy merging RAG and knowledge graphs, and (4) a standardized model for industrial knowledge representation.

title: Point cloud registration for non-destructive, high-resolution coating thickness measurement from 3D scans
abstract: Thickness is a key specification property of thermal spray coatings. The ability to measure coating thickness nondestructively, in situ, and with high spatial resolution is thus vital for applications like process monitoring, quality assurance, and research. To this end, one of few promising approaches is 3D scanning. By capturing the workpiece before and after coating, thickness can be inferred from the difference in geometry. However, a major challenge stems from the relatively low thickness of typical coatings, which necessitates an exceptionally precise surface registration. We present a complete algorithmic pipeline for non-destructive thickness measurement using optical 3D scanners, suitable for thermal spraying. At the core, we propose an alignment algorithm that registers both scans to an a priori known CAD model. This indirect approach eliminates the need for post-processing of the measured point clouds. A novel weighting scheme accounts for local mismatches in point density of the scans, enabling high accuracy even on incomplete scans. We demonstrate the method on several applications, like spray spot analysis and quality assessment of a production part, and validate the accuracy of the method. Additionally, we provide detailed analyses of convergence properties and the effects of measurement noise, point density, and model mismatch.
